metadata.title: PISA 2012 Results: Students and Money (Volume VI) (EN)

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This OECD PISA 2012 volume reports results based on the PISA 2012 assessment of 15-year-olds across participating countries and economies, using the PISA sampling framework and quality controls described in the technical annexes (Annex A2 and Annex A4). For school-level questionnaire responses, the report states that principals’ responses are weighted to be proportionate to the number of 15-year-olds enrolled in the school, indicating the use of complex survey weighting for school-level estimates. The excerpt provided does not specify the exact student weight variable names (e.g., TOTWGT/W_FSTUWT) or whether replicate weights (e.g., BRR/jackknife) were used, so the precise weighting implementation cannot be confirmed from the text shown. For analysts using the PISA database, the standard approach is to apply the provided sampling weights and replicate weights (if available) when estimating standard errors and country comparisons, and to use the PISA scaling procedures for the financial literacy scale.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The provided text does not describe an analysis model that uses plausible values (PVs) for a student-level cognitive outcome, nor does it document a specific missing-data handling procedure for the reported financial literacy results. Instead, the excerpt explains the PISA reporting conventions for missing data symbols (e.g., categories not applying, too few observations, data not available/withdrawn, or excessive missingness), which is a publication reporting scheme rather than an imputation/deletion method. Therefore, missing-data handling is treated as not reported for this extraction because the excerpt does not specify whether missing questionnaire items were imputed, deleted, or otherwise handled in the estimation of scale scores and indicators.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The volume reports results from the PISA 2012 financial literacy assessment, which was optional for countries. The excerpt states that the financial literacy assessment was administered to approximately 29,000 students in 13 OECD countries and economies (Australia, the Flemish Community of Belgium, the Czech Republic, Estonia, France, Israel, Italy, New Zealand, Poland, the Slovak Republic, Slovenia, Spain and the United States) and five partner countries and economies (Colombia, Croatia, Latvia, the Russian Federation and Shanghai-China). The excerpt does not provide additional analytic-sample filtering rules (e.g., specific exclusions for missing questionnaire items, grade restrictions beyond the PISA target population, or task completion thresholds) for the financial literacy analyses; it therefore cannot be further specified from the provided text.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD PISA 2012 volume (Volume VI) reports the first international assessment of financial literacy for 15-year-olds. The financial literacy assessment was administered to approximately 29,000 students in 18 participating countries and economies (13 OECD countries/economies plus 5 partners), with paper-based testing and a total test time of about two hours per student. Financial literacy proficiency is reported using proficiency levels (e.g., Level 5 as top performers) and summary indicators such as mean scores, shares of lowest performers (Level 1 or below), and shares of top performers (Level 5 or above). The report also compares financial literacy with mathematics and reading performance and examines relationships with student background and attitudes (e.g., socio-economic status, immigrant background, and learning attitudes). The excerpt emphasizes that PISA cannot identify cause-and-effect relationships, and it provides PISA-specific conventions for missing data reporting, but it does not document a specific missing-data handling or PV estimation procedure in the provided text.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This document is an OECD PISA results volume rather than an empirical machine-learning study. The excerpt provides descriptive and comparative results (means, proficiency levels, and associations) and explains PISA’s assessment design, target population, and missing-data reporting symbols, but it does not present an ML modeling pipeline, PV estimation strategy, or a documented missing-data handling method for the reported indicators. As a result, ML technique fields and structured predictive findings are intentionally left empty, and PV/missing-data handling are treated as not applicable/not reported for this extraction based on the provided text.
